paragraphs: BoldInBeauty is a 3D gacha game in Unreal Engine 5.8. The public repository is a development snapshot: the C++ demo, a Node account server, the asset catalogue, and the AI production scripts. It is not a finished store build. Guest play does not need the account server.

The published summon table is 78% 3-star, 19.9% 4-star, 2% 5-star, and 0.1% 6-star. Featured banners in the demo notes are Judge at 5-star and Narrator at 6-star. Within a rarity, Standard splits that rarity’s chance equally. A 10-pull guarantees one 4-star. Pity is one 5-star per 100 rolls and one 6-star per 2,000, and Daily pulls do not count toward those.

The screenshots are from the public demo captures: the hub, combat, summoning, equipment, a chapter fight, and a Neo Tokyo blockout. The hub itself marks its currency figures as placeholders in BIBConfig.h and BIBTuning.h, so this page does not treat those figures as the economy.
callout: Purchased marketplace packs are not in the snapshot. Greybox rebuilds that need them are documented and wait until you supply packs you own.

paragraphs: Agent Fitness is the other working flagship, beside Agent Arena. In AI Colosseum it is the training ground and the choose-your-fighter roster. One task — a prompt plus attachments — is sent to many models and modes. The brief names GPT, Claude, Kimi, Gemini, and CLI agents such as Claude Code and Codex.

Each run gets a fitness score: time, tokens, cost, and success, measured automatically. A person's judgement carries 50% of the weight. The best setups meet in single-elimination tournaments with Elo. Mixed-provider pipelines (planner, executor, critic) are scored as one unit. System prompts evolve by mutation and crossover, and the lineage is kept.

The lab is a working MVP and it runs locally. The job queue is Postgres: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, with leases, heartbeats, a worker pool, per-provider token buckets, and retries with backoff. CLI agents are sandboxed in Docker with no network. API keys are Fernet-encrypted. Roles are admin, reviewer, and viewer, with audit logs.

paragraphs: ScopeHound is an attack-surface map for a domain you are allowed to look at. It gathers certificate-transparency names from crt.sh, resolves DNS, probes HTTP and TLS lightly, fingerprints the stack, and checks security headers. Every asset gets a risk score. Reports come out as HTML, Markdown, and JSON.
An optional local model, through Ollama, writes a plain-language summary. With no model, a template does it, so the tool still runs offline and does not call a paid service.
A live scan will not start without --i-am-authorised, and requests are rate limited. ScopeHound maps and advises. It does not exploit, brute-force credentials, or send attack payloads.
callout: The figure is the offline --demo report. The banner says synthetic data. It is not a scan of a real target. Do not read the host names, addresses, or scores in it as findings.

paragraphs: Snitchless tells you what a Linux laptop is saying to the network: which apps connect out, which companies and countries those flows point at, which trackers show up, what is listening, which Flatpak apps hold broad permissions, and how Firefox, SSH, and the firewall are set. The result is a score from 0 to 100 and a list of findings in plain language.
Fixes are dry-run unless you explicitly apply them, and they are reversible. The tool is standard-library Python, MIT licensed, with 9 tests. It is for the machine you own or administer.

title: FiaHealth
summary: Fia Health 0.2.0. A local-first health workspace: one encrypted vault per profile, a scrypt login, and tests for isolation and throttling. No records are shown.
highlight: v0.2.0 · encrypted vaults · scrypt login · private
stage: Local-first. Private. Not linked. No personal data.

facts.label: Version
facts.value: 0.2.0, 29 October 2026. No cloud storage and no Apple Health.

facts.label: Vaults
facts.value: Each profile has its own encrypted vault. The server stores only the ciphertext.

facts.label: Login
facts.value: The browser sends a login token derived from the passphrase, with a salt separate from the vault key. The server keeps a scrypt hash. It never sees the passphrase or a readable record.

facts.label: Session
facts.value: A 12-hour HttpOnly cookie. Five wrong tries, then a five-minute lock.

facts.label: Vault key
facts.value: PBKDF2-SHA256, 600,000 iterations, a random 16-byte salt, then a non-exportable AES-256-GCM key. Each save uses a fresh 12-byte nonce.

facts.label: Writes
facts.value: Checked against the vault version so two devices cannot silently overwrite each other.

facts.label: Network
facts.value: Listens on 127.0.0.1 only. Signing in needs the local server. Internet is not required.

facts.label: Tests
facts.value: Account isolation, wrong passphrases, throttling, and cross-site writes. The browser test uses synthetic records, not a real profile.

facts.label: Records
facts.value: Daily check-ins, cycle notes without fertility predictions, medications and appointments, and a personal funding ledger. Remaining funds are a planning figure, not an official balance. None of those records are shown here.

facts.label: Repository
facts.value: Private. Not linked.

paragraphs: Fia Health 0.2.0 is a local-first workspace beside FiaOS. Each profile has its own passphrase and its own encrypted vault. There is no subscription and no cloud copy. This page describes the architecture. It does not name anyone and it does not show a record.

Login is checked by the local server. A scrypt hash of a login token is what the server stores. The vault key is separate: PBKDF2-SHA256 with 600,000 iterations, then AES-256-GCM. A wrong passphrase is rejected. Five failures impose a five-minute lock. Tests cover isolation between profiles, throttling, and cross-site writes.
The server listens only on localhost. The repository is private and is not linked. There is no screenshot.

paragraphs: medlib is an offline suite for studying medicine in Australia, from premed through residency. Search is hybrid: BM25 on SQLite FTS5 plus local embeddings, with medical abbreviation expansion. About 37,000 cards come back in 50–130 milliseconds. Ask mode uses a local model and cites the source it used.

Around that: a pathway dashboard from Year 12 toward specialist training, a planner with Pomodoro blocks, spaced review, and streaks, a quiz, wellbeing reminders, a rotation case log, UCAT and GAMSAT timers that follow official section timings, and 10 clinical calculators.

The app is Python and Flask, with fastembed, NumPy, and Ollama, and a vanilla JS front end. It is a working local prototype and a personal tool. A separate pipeline builds NotebookLM source packs from Anki exports. The packs are not shown here. Flashcard contents are not shown either.
